articles.title: WWE Raw Live Updates, Results, Highlights From Usos vs. 946 and More After Money in the Bank 2026
articles.summary: Welcome to Bleacher Report's live coverage of WWE Raw on October 12.
articles.body:
Welcome to Bleacher Report's live coverage of WWE Raw on October 12.

Scroll down for updates from throughout the show.

Raw ended with 946 standing over their fallen enemies. Keys, Hayes, Parker, Nima and Price might not have won the match, but they won the battle for sure.

When the show returned, the match had actually gotten under control to some degree. Four men were on the apron while Nima and Jimmy fought in the ring as the legal men.

Jimmy took a lot of damage as 946 kept him away from his teammates. The pace had slowed considerably, and now they were taking their time. Jimmy fired off a kick to give himself a chance to make a tag.

Jey came in to help and hit a Spear, which allowed Jimmy to tag in Solo right as Keys tagged in, too. The former friends fought, and Sikoa hit a nice Samoan drop to take him down.

Parker yanked the ref out of the ring as Solo was about to get the pin, and she threw him over the barricade to get rid of him. OTM and The Usos fought into the crowd. Keys cleared off the announce table to prepare for something.

He used the steel steps, but we didn't get to see it because the camera was on the Usos. Jey climbed up to the second level and took out OTM with a huge dive, but Jimmy went down, too.

Keys ended up being put through the table with a Samoan drop once Solo recovered. As Sikoa set up for the Samoan Spike, a masked man appeared out of nowhere and hit him with a crowbar. He revealed himself to be Carmelo Hayes.

946 completely decimated The Usos and Solo. The match really didn't matter anymore. There was no ref to count anyway.

946 made their way through the crowd as boos echoed in the arena as we prepared for the main event. Jaida Parker, Bronco Nima, Lucien Price and Royce Keys sat on the announce table as they waited for Solo, Jimmy and Jey to come out.

Parker talked a lot of trash from the apron as the guys stood on either side of the ring. The crowd broke into a Yeet chant as the two groups stared each other down.

All six men started brawling, so the ref called for the bell to get things underway. This wasn't officially under tornado rules, but it may as well have been. The Usos and OTM fought while Keys and Solo took it out of the ring.

Keys threw Sikoa over the barricade and then helped OTM get the upper hand over the twins. Solo threw an office chair into Keys' face as he recovered. All hell was breaking lose as Jimmy hit Whisper in the Wind from the top rope to the floor to take everyone down.

Ethan Page attacked Rey Fenix backstage, but Chad Gable showed up to drive him off.

WWE gave them a lot of time, so they worked through another break into the next segment. They continued to make this a competitive and exciting match.

Gable grabbed Fenix and hit three German suplexes in a row for a two-count. Fenix recovered and hit a few high-flying moves in a row, but it wasn't enough to put the champion away.

The masked man ran across the top rope for a kick to the face, followed by a huge frog splash for another near-fall. Gable put him back in the Ankle Lock and after several close calls, Fenix finally got to the ropes to force a break.

Gable hit a German suplex that sent the back of Fenix's head into the top turnbuckle, but then Fenix tripped Gable off the top rope when he stumbled into it. He tried to grab Gable for the Mexican Muscle Buster, but he was too injured.

Gable countered and put him back in the Ankle Lock to finally get the submission win.

This was an outstanding match. Definitely make sure you check this one out if you did not watch the show live. Both guys were awesome.

The show came back as Gable countered a double underhook. He caught Fenix coming in off a springboard and hit a northern lights suplex for a two-count. They kept the pace quick as Gable hit a moonsault for a near-fall.

The champ was able to apply an Ankle Lock, but Fenix was quick to counter out of it with some kicks. He and Gable continued to go counter for counter, with neither man able to string more than a couple of moves together in a row.

Gable caught Fenix in the middle of a jump to hit an Angle Slam for two. Fenix started to build some momentum, but Gable hit a belly-to-belly throw into the barricade to stop him. When they got back in the ring, Fenix hit a nice cutter for a two-count.

Iyo Sky almost got into a fight with Judgment Day backstage before asking Adam Pearce for a match. She and Pearce walked away to discuss it. Up next, Chad Gable came out for his IC title defense against Rey Fenix.

Fenix and Gable locked up and started with a standard sequence. A headlock into a drop toe hold kickstarted some takedowns and counters from both men. They came to a stalemate and reset before shaking hands and trading punches.

Rey sent Chad out of the ring and hit a moonsault from the middle rope to the floor to send us into a break.

The Usos and Solo Sikoa had a quick segment backstage before the break. When the show returned, the crowd was loudly chanting Oba Femi's name before his music hit and he made his entrance.

Femi said he is in a great mood after beating Bronson Reed at Money in the Bank. He said the one thing that matters is that everyone will bend the knee to The Ruler.

Paul Heyman came out and said he warned Reed about Femi that it would take a ton of Tsunamis to beat him, but he only hit one. He called Femi the first man to kick out of it.

He said he agrees with everything Oba has said, and he is the future of WWE. Femi took the mic from Heyman and tossed it away. Heyman immediately looked terrified, but Oba said he is not Brock Lesnar or Roman Reigns.

He said he is not a Paul Heyman guy before dropping the mic and leaving the ring peacefully.

We returned to see Perez attempt a side Russian leg sweep, but Green countered and hit a few arm drags with an enziguiri at the end. She hit the Rough Ryder, but only got a two-count.

Roxy made a comeback and got a close two-count with a shining wizard. The crowd began chanting for Chelsea as she got to her feet. She dropped Perez with a German suplex, but Morgan grabbed her feet to distract her.

Perez used it to her advantage to hit an uppercut, but Green blocked the moonsault and sent her into Raquel to knock her off the apron. She hit a suicide dive to take out both women at once, and she sent Liv over the announce table when she came to attack her.

When she got back in the ring, Perez hit Pop Rox for the pin and the win.

Beating a world champion means Perez may have just earned herself a future title shot. Judgment Day continued to beat up Green after the match, and with Tiffany Stratton out with an injury, there was nobody to come help her.

We returned from the break to see the match already going and the women struggling for control at ringside. They got back into the ring to avoid a countout, and Green took control with a few arm wrenches.

Chelsea blew Morgan a kiss after slapping the taste out of Roxy's mouth. She nailed a huge missile dropkick as the show cut to a break.

After the break, Liv Morgan came out with the rest of Judgment Day to celebrate regaining the world title from Stephanie Vaquer at MITB.

Before much could be said, Chelsea Green's music hit and she came to the ring. She said she came out to congratulate her ahead of their Crown Jewel showdown. Morgan laughed in her face and refused to shake her hand.

She insulted Green up and down, calling her a fake champion. Chelsea said she is fine with being underestimated because everyone has been doing it her entire career.

Roxanne Perez got in Chelsea's face, so Green issued a challenge for a match. A ref showed up, so it looks like we are getting this right away.

Adam Pearce was shown telling referee Chad Patton that he knows the main event will be chaotic, so he just needs him to make sure there is a pin or submission and then get out. He made sure to tell him this is not a punishment; he just needs a senior referee.

We returned to see Cass still dominating the luchador, but Rey began to fight back after countering a suplex with a knee to the head. With one big shot, Cass put him down for a two-count.

Mysterio fought out of a powerbomb and took the big man down before sending him out of the ring. He hit the 619 to the back of Cass' head, followed by a diving DDT on the floor.

Rey hit another 619 to his leg as he tried to get back into the ring, but when he went for the normal 619, Cass caught him with a big elbow.

The ref almost disqualified Cass when he refused to let up in the corner. She checked on Rey and Dragon Lee appeared out of nowhere to deliver a kick to Cass while the ref was distracted. Rey hit the 619 and used a victory roll to get the pin.

The first match of the night saw Rey Mysterio battle Big Cass. Rey used his quickness to avoid the giant early in the match after their initial clash.

He hid under the ring and came back out in a different spot to surprise him with a hurricanrana from the apron. He dropkicked Cass out of the ring, but then the big man pulled him out and drove him into the barricade.

Penta came to the ring with a fancy custom briefcase that had his logos and Money in the Bank written in Spanish. The crowd gave him a warm welcome.

Penta talked about being proud to have won the MITB briefcase, and he told the champions to watch their back, because he plans to become a world champion.

It seemed like Penta had wrapped up his promo when Je'Von Evans came out limping with a sling on his arm. He is really selling the severity of the huge bump he took from the ladder through the ambulance roof.

Evans said if anybody deserves the briefcase, it's Penta, and he is proud of him. As they hugged, Bron Breakker showed up and Speared the injured Evans.

Breakker walked away slowly as official rushed to the ring to help Evans.

The show opened with some Money in the Bank highlights. After the usual shots of people walking around in and outside the arena, When we went live in the arena, Penta made his way out to celebrate winning MITB.

articles.title: WWE Raw Winners, Live Grades, Reaction and Highlights After Money in the Bank 2026
articles.summary: On the heels of Penta and Tiffany Stratton winning the Men's and Women's Money in the Bank Ladder Matches, respectively, WWE Raw rolled into Bossier City, Louisiana, with a show headlined by the latest chapter in the rivalry between The Bloodline and 946.
articles.body:
On the heels of Penta and Tiffany Stratton winning the Men's and Women's Money in the Bank Ladder Matches, respectively, WWE Raw rolled into Bossier City, Louisiana, with a show headlined by the latest chapter in the rivalry between The Bloodline and 946.

What went down when those two factions squared off in a high-intensity six-man tag match?

Find out the answer to that and more in this recap of the October 12 show, including live grades and analysis.

Announced in advance for Monday's show were:

The Usos and Solo Sikoa vs. Royce Keys, Bronco Nima, and Lucien Price

Intercontinental Championship Match: Rey Fenix vs. Chad Gable (c)

An appearance from Mr. Money in the Bank, Penta

Last Time in Action: Penta won the Money in the Bank Ladder Match (Money in the Bank, October 11)

The triumphant Penta kicked off the show, still in celebration mode following his potentially career-altering victory Saturday night in New Orleans.

He addressed the fans, saying that if he chooses to cash in, he will be a world champion.

Je'Von Evans interrupted and joined his frequent tag team partner in the ring. Clearly still banged up from the jaw-dropping bump he took from the top of a ladder through the roof of an ambulance, The Young OG dapped up his friend and told him he was proud of him.

Bron Breakker came from out of nowhere, spearing Evans, who shoved Penta out of the way. Medics checked on the babyface as The Badass made his exit.

It was shocking how much this opening segment was not about Penta, despite him kicking the show off.

Evans showing toughness and still coming to work despite his injuries is a great call. It endears him to the fans, as we saw based on their reaction to his insistence that he be there.

There was not much to this segment other than re-establishing Breakker as an unstoppable force after he fell short on Saturday. While there is still time and opportunity, there are only so many of these types of segments that WWE can continue to produce before Breakker earns the reputation of a runner-up rather than the guy.

Last Time In Action: Big Cass defeated Sean Legacy (Main Event, October 8); Rey Mysterio and Dragon Lee lost to Dominik Mysterio and JD McDonagh (Raw, October 5)

Big Cass' war with the former LWO continued Monday as he squared off with Rey Mysterio.

The Hall of Famer got clever early, outsmarting the big man, but fell victim to his strength and size advantage. The big man dominated the competition, even finding ways to stunt the offensive momentum of the former world champion.

It was an admonishment from referee Jessika Carr, an undetected kick from Dragon Lee, and a victory roll from Mysterio that proved Cass' downfall as the greatest luchador of all time, earning the come-from-behind victory.

Rarely pretty, this was a clash of styles for sure, but the story execution was handled well. Big Cass was protected, dominating the match and leaving little question as to who the real winner should have been. Mysterio won only after the heel's ego got the best of him and Lee earned a little revenge for his recent treatment.

Carr standing up to Cass and backing him down was a nice touch and something we need more of. She has the authority and should be able to flex it in matches beyond those involving Becky Lynch.

Is the bloom off the rose that is Cass at this point? A loss to Lee and Mysterio have seemingly hampered his momentum.

Last Time in Action: Liv Morgan defeated Stephanie Vaquer and Becky Lynch (Money in the Bank, October 11); Roxanne Perez lost the Money in the Bank Ladder Match (Money in the Bank, October 11)

Liv Morgan celebrated her latest Women's World Championship victory Monday night alongside her Judgment Day family, pyro and all.

She claimed that her attention was now on becoming the first two-time Crown Jewel champion. That brought out Chelsea Green, the WWE Women's Champion and SmackDown Superstar.

The Hot Mess listened as Morgan criticized her, taking shots at her for not being a fighting champion and revealing that her backup, Money in the Bank winner Tiffany Stratton, was injured.

Green called Morgan the "placeholder girlfriend" of Dominik Mysterio before Roxanne Perez interrupted and issued a challenge for a match.

This was exactly what it needed to be: an introduction to a short-term program that set the tone right out of the gate. Who knows what the future holds for the Crown Jewel premium live event but if it does take place in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, the women's Crown Jewel Championship match is set.

Perez interjecting herself and standing up to Green was a nice look at the increasingly confident Prodigy. A confident Perez who may or may not, eventually, look to relieve Morgan of her own title.

Last Time in Action: Perez lost the titular ladder match (Money in the Bank, October 11); Chelsea Green, Paige, and Tiffany Stratton lost to Fatal Influence (SmackDown, September 25)

Green and Perez battled in singles competition, the result of the earlier confrontation.

Green showed great fire and had the fans behind her vs. Perez, but The Prodigy ultimately took control. When the Hot Mess fought from underneath late, she had the momentum.

She wiped out Raquel Rodriguez with a tope suicida on the floor, then sent Liv Morgan flying over the announce table. Red hot, she re-entered the squared circle, only to succumb to Pop Rox as Perez capitalized on the distraction and earned a big win.

After the match, Green smacked a taunting Morgan, only to endure a beatdown by The Judgment Day. The heels stood tall to close the segment.

Joe Tessitore added some great analysis on the headset, noting that being a champion often makes a competitor 25 percent better, which may help explain Green's recent improvement.

Perez and Green have wrestled each other only once on WWE TV, in a May 7, 2024 NXT Championship Match. It showed as the timing and chemistry were not necessary there early on.

Green straight YEET'ed Morgan across the announce table. It made for a great visual and explained the distraction that ultimately cost the babyface.

Last Time in Action: Oba Femi defeated Bronson Reed (Money in the Bank, October 11)

Fresh off an emphatic victory over Bronson Reed, Oba Femi addressed the WWE Universe.

He made it clear that it doesn't matter how many teammates or cousins someone has; everyone will bend the knee. He teased, leaving The Vision in the rearview mirror, "on the road to destiny."

Paul Heyman interrupted and joined Femi in the squared circle, claiming his performance Saturday night against Reed was the best of the year so far. Before the Wise Man could butter him up any more, Femi threw the Hall of Famer's microphone out of the ring and said he is not like Brock Lesnar and Roman Reigns. They were Paul Heyman guys.

The Ruler left the advocate in the ring as he exited.

The teases of Heyman joining forces with Femi have gone on for months so it was nice, on this first night on the road to Survivor Series, that The Ruler cleared up all confusion by denouncing the Hall of Famer and announcing he was a lone wolf in WWE.

Heyman's facial expressions remain among the most underrated, underappreciated elements on WWE TV.

Intercontinental Championship Match: Chad Gable vs. Rey Fenix

Last Time In Action: Chad Gable defeated Rey Fenix (Raw, September 14); Rey Fenix defeated Ethan Page (Raw, October 5)

Chad Gable's latest Intercontinental Championship defense came against one of WWE's hottest workhorses: AAA Cruiserweight Champion Rey Fenix.

As expected, given the competitors involved, the two delivered a competitive match in which neither man established a sustained advantage.

At one point, Gable folded Fenix up at ringside, only for the challenger to catch him with a cutter back inside the squared circle for a close two-count.

A huge hurricanrana off the top rope, followed by an Asai Moonsault, earned Fenix another near-fall. Adios Amigos and a frog splash again earned Fenix a tremendously close two-count.

Gable kept targeting Fenix's ankle, and the luchador fought through the pain several times, clawing and scratching toward the ropes for sanctuary. Late, Fenix hoisted the champion up for a Mexican Muscle Buster, but his leg gave out and Gable reapplied the submission, eventually forcing the tapout from the AAA Cruiserweight Champion.

An absolute banger of a match that should surprise no one, considering who was involved. The reversals and counters were creative. The drama was heightened and the crowd got behind all of it.

Gable winning was the right call for now, but Fenix will win over the WWE Universe the same way his brother did.

With Gable holding the title, the Intercontinental Championship is quickly becoming WWE's work-rate title. With this and his defense against Dragon Lee, Gable has been on fire in the ring.

Last Time in Action: LA Knight and Solo Sikoa fought The Usos to a no contest (Raw, August 24); 946 has not competed as a unit on WWE TV

After weeks of intensifying violence and chaos, The Bloodline and the 946 squared off in a blockbuster six-man tag match to close out Raw.

The heels isolated Jimmy Uso for much of the match, but a hot tag to Solo Sikoa sparked a babyface comeback for The Bloodline. As the babyfaces built momentum, Jaida Parker sent referee Chad Patton over the guardrail and into the crowd to prevent a loss.

With the Usos, Bronco Nima, and Lucien Price battling in the crowd, Royce Keys prepared the commentary table. Jey Uso dove from the stands onto his opponents, then Parker soared through the air to wipe him and his brother out.

Back at ringside, Sikoa delivered a Samoan Drop to Keys through the announce table and set up for the finish.

A big splashback in the ring, and Samoan Spike seemed to put Sikoa in position to win the match for The Bloodline, only for Carmelo Hayes to stun the WWE Universe by revealing he was the latest member of 946.

The heel faction brutalized the opposition, leaving them lying on the mat to close out the show.

946 entered to no theme music and it was the perfect choice. It conveyed the group's unpredictability and do-whatever-we-want attitude. Having entrance music cued up only takes away from the anything-can-happen element of the faction. It is surprising it took this long for the production team to figure that out.

And just like that, Hayes has new life in WWE after being left for dead after being left off the WrestleMania card.

The moment Naomi returns to take Parker out will result in a generational pop.

This was the single most important match on the show; the one that everyone the entire show was sold on. It delivered the expected chaos, with a great twist, and another week of the heels standing tall. The question now? When will Roman Reigns step into this war?

The Intercontinental Championship Match was phenomenal. Gable and Fenix tore the house down in the night's best match, setting an impossibly high bar for any match to eclipse. It was another extraordinary performance from Gable and Fenix, continuing to build that all-important connection with the audience.

This was good enough to warrant a rematch sooner rather than later.

Through the first half of the show, this was headed toward a solid "C+" grade, but the IC title match and the show-closing main-event brawl elevated it and put a nice bow on it.

That there was hype for Crown Jewel, along with a few story threads set in place for the weeks to come, only helped make this one a relative success, following the high-profile Money in the Bank premium live event.

articles.title: Carmelo Hayes Turns Heel, Helps 946 Beat Bloodline in Major Surprise on WWE Raw
articles.summary: Competing in their first match as a group, 946's Royce Keys and OTM defeated The Bloodline's Solo Sikoa and The Usos in a six-man tag team bout Monday night on Raw.
articles.body:
Competing in their first match as a group, 946's Royce Keys and OTM defeated The Bloodline's Solo Sikoa and The Usos in a six-man tag team bout Monday night on Raw.

In a shocking turn of events, Carmelo Hayes turned heel and joined 946 to help them take down The Bloodline.

Last month, 946 debuted as a stable by interrupting a tag team match pitting LA Knight and Sikoa against The Usos. Keys and OTM attacked all four of the combatants in the match and ended Raw in chaos.

In the weeks that followed, 946 made it clear that their goal was to eradicate The Bloodline due to the fact that Bloodline member Jacob Fatu had put Keys on the shelf for a few weeks after a street fight between them.

Keys and OTM sent a message to The Bloodline by setting their vehicle on fire, and they followed that up by seemingly attempting to pick off Bloodline members one by one.

It started with Solo, who they attacked and kidnapped before dropping him in the middle of nowhere. Then, 946 shocked the wrestling world with what they did to Fatu on the Sept. 28 episode of Raw.

At the end of the show, a vehicle went speeding toward Fatu after he brawled with Keys in the parking garage, and hit him, sending him flying through the air.

Jaida Parker exited the vehicle after hitting The Samoan Werewolf, acting as if it was an accident.

However, Parker changed her tone and declared that, "nobody's safe," before getting into a vehicle with Keys and driving off, signaling her alignment with 946.

Raw general manager Adam Pearce declared the following week that 946 would face The Bloodline in a six-man tag on Oct. 12, and while The Usos expected Roman Reigns to be their partner, Reigns revealed that it would be the returning Sikoa instead.

Although The Usos did make an attempt to save Solo from getting kidnapped, it was fair to wonder how they would coexist, given their recent feud with their brother.

Keys and OTM proved to be a strong unit on Monday, as 946 prevailed in its first official match by taking down The Bloodline.

articles.title: ISSF World Cup: Rhythm Sangwan misses bronze, Indian rifle men fail to enter final
articles.summary: PUNE: It was a no-podium day for Indians at the ISSF World Cup in Cairo as both, pistol and rifle shooters failed to show their best on Monday.
articles.body: PUNE: It was a no-podium day for Indians at the ISSF World Cup in Cairo as both, pistol and rifle shooters failed to show their best on Monday.Barring Rhythm Sangwan, who finished fourth in women’s 25m sports pistol final, other five Indians couldn’t even enter the finals of their respective categories.Rhythm, the Paris Games participant, missed the bronze by two hits in the final that was won by Singapore’s Xiu Yi Teh. The silver and bronze were won by France's Heloise Fourre and Bulgaria's Miroslava Mincheva, respectively. Rhythm, 22, scored 26 in the final and was in medal contention till the seventh series.She looked good to seal the bronze, at least, but in the eighth series, the Haryana shooter missed four out of five shots, while Miroslava, who was a point behind Rhythm, went two points ahead to push the Indian for elimination.Earlier, Rhythm qualified for the final on top, by scoring 587 in the qualifier. In 2023, the Indian had broken the 29-year-old record in the event by scoring 595 at the World Cup in Baku. The previous record was held by Bulgarian shooter Diana Iorgova, who had shot 594 in Milan World Cup in May 1994. However, the Indian went out of form after a dismal show in the Paris Olympics.“It was a good match. I am happy about the way I shot in the qualification round and then in the final. I just had one bad series and that happened to be the last one. Unfortunately, I couldn’t win the medal, but I am satisfied with the way I shot,” Rhythm, who has played in only two international tournaments since Paris, told TOI.“I think such days give you confidence for the future,” she added.Other Indians in fray, Divya TS (582) and Chinki Yadav (580), finished 10th and 16th, respectively.In the men’s 10m air rifle event, Paris Games fourth-place finisher, Arjun Babuta failed to enter the final after finishing 16th with a score of 630. Other Indians, Dhanush Srikanth (629.4) and Paarth Makhija (629.3) were placed 21st and 22nd, respectively.

articles.title: From introduction to skeet gun at 13 to Asian Games bronze: Parinaz Dhaliwal’s journey of precision, perseverance and the right support
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: For Parinaaz Dhaliwal, success in skeet shooting is about much more than hitting targets.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For Parinaaz Dhaliwal, success in skeet shooting is about much more than hitting targets. It is a combination of technical precision, mental strength, financial backing and the ability to find balance under pressure. After years of investing in her game, the Asian Games medallist believes experience, the right coaching environment and an unwavering support system have helped her take significant strides forward.When Parinaaz looks back at her journey in shooting, she does not attribute her progress to one competition, one coach or one breakthrough moment. Instead, she sees it as an evolution shaped by years of training, international exposure and lessons learnt along the way. The bronze medal in the women’s skeet team event at the Asian Games 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya in Japan alongside Raiza Dhillon and Maheshwari Chauhan, was a significant milestone in that journey.“It was bits of everything, to be honest,” she says, reflecting on the difference between her previous Asian Games appearance and the latest campaign. “You evolve with every single competition. You learn something or the other. You win or you don’t win, but you always learn.”The medal was the culmination of a more comprehensive preparation programme, one that she believes made a tangible difference. Ahead of the Games, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), in coordination with the National Rifle Association of India (NRAI), organised two preparatory camps. The first, held in Aug, focused on fundamentals, while the Sept camp concentrated on fine-tuning and final preparations.The support structure, she says, was also stronger than before, with foreign coaching expertise and a larger team of support staff contributing to the preparations.An important part of that preparation was the presence of her personal coach, Anthony, an Olympic medallist from France. She received permission from the federation to have him join the national camp and accompany her to Japan, where he worked alongside national coaches and foreign coach Riccardo Filippelli.For her, the arrangement was about more than technical advice. A personal coach who has worked with an athlete over an extended period understands the individual beyond the shooting range, including their habits, temperament and response to pressure.“My personal coach might have seen my tantrums or might have seen a lot,” she says with a laugh. “He has seen various sides of me because I train with him a lot more than I do with my national coach.”She is particularly appreciative of the cooperation between the coaches, describing the atmosphere as one without ego or insecurity. Anthony, she adds, was equally conscious of respecting the national coaching structure.Her introduction to shooting began well before she took up skeet seriously. Growing up around firearms, she was familiar with the sport, and her father, Ratandeep Dhaliwal, encouraged her to learn how to use a weapon. At Mayo College Girls’ School in Ajmer, she participated in open-sight shooting competitions and school-level events.When she turned 13, her father suggested that she explore shotgun shooting. She initially tried trap, but it was an unexpected session at the skeet range that changed her trajectory.During a week at home to prepare for a state competition, her mentor, Amarjang Singh Sidhu, suggested that she try a station of skeet. She hit a couple of targets and immediately found herself drawn to the discipline.“I looked at my dad and said, ‘Papa, I think I want to do skeet.’ He was like, ‘Huh?’” she recalls.Her father discussed the decision with her grandfather, and by the following day, she had a skeet gun.“It turned out to be a great decision,” she says. While she remains close to several trap shooters, skeet is the discipline she finds more engaging. The experience reinforced a lesson she considers fundamental to sporting success: an athlete must enjoy what they do.Behind the medals, however, lies a challenge that is often overlooked: the financial demands of competitive shooting.Shotgun shooting, she explains, can be particularly expensive, making financial stability and institutional support crucial for aspiring athletes. Equipment, training and travel can place a substantial burden on families, while sponsorships often arrive only after an athlete has established a record.Despite having competed at the previous Asian Games, she says she relied on her family to fund her development for years, even while working with internationally accomplished coaches, fitness professionals and sports psychologists.She is grateful for the backing, but is equally conscious of the sacrifices that preceded it. Her father had travelled with her to competitions and camps, both in India and abroad. This year, however, he stepped back from travelling because her grandparents were unwell and needed family support.“I said, for me and for my mental sanity, it’s just better that you are at home with my grandparents. And I’m fine,” she says, drawing on the independence she developed during her years at boarding school.For young shooters, she believes, understanding the financial realities of the sport is as important as recognising their own potential.Parinaaz’s preparation has evolved beyond technique and equipment. Over the past three years, she has worked extensively on fitness and the technical aspects of her shooting, while also consulting a sports psychologist based in the UK.At the elite level, she believes, every component matters. “You cannot leave anything unattended at all,” she said.One incident from the World Cup in Lonato, Italy, illustrates the importance she places on mental preparation. After the first four rounds, she was uncertain about her standing and found herself worrying about the competition. Anthony responded by taking her out for dinner rather than allowing her anxiety to dominate the evening.She was initially concerned about losing sleep ahead of the following morning’s round. Her coach, however, believed that continuing to dwell on the competition would be counterproductive.The evening continued with a walk by the lake and gelato, helping her shift her attention away from the scoreboard and reconnect with the reasons she had taken up shooting.Anthony, she said, believes strongly in maintaining balance and reminding athletes why they compete in the first place.The next day, she shot a perfect round of 25, her best of the competition, which helped her reach a shoot-off.“These are the small things that coaches with experience can teach you,” she said.At the Asian Games, the women's team faced a difficult opening day, but the athletes concentrated on their individual routines rather than becoming distracted by the collective result.Skeet may have a team component, but the discipline demands individual accountability. Each shooter must execute their own process, manage pressure and remain focused on the target in front of them.The team's positive atmosphere helped them persevere, while the men's skeet team also produced a strong finish. India ultimately returned with medals in both the men's and women's team events.For her, the result reflected not only individual ability but also the value of a supportive environment in which athletes and coaches worked towards a common objective.She also believes India's development in skeet coaching needs greater attention. While the country has several accomplished coaches in trap, she sees a relative shortage of experienced specialists in skeet. International coaches, despite their high fees, can offer technical knowledge and an understanding of competitive pressure acquired through years at the highest level.At the same time, she acknowledges that being an accomplished shooter does not automatically make someone an accomplished coach. Coaching, she says, is a discipline in itself.Looking ahead, she intends to continue building on the progress she has made through competition experience, technical refinement and mental preparation. Her latest Asian Games performance is a milestone, but not the end of the journey.For a shooter whose career began with a spontaneous decision at 13, the larger lesson remains remarkably simple: excellence comes from getting the fundamentals right, learning from every competition and finding the people who help you become better.And perhaps that is what defines Parinaaz’s journey best. The targets may be fleeting, but the work behind each shot is anything but.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: The complex issue of egg-freezing in sport
articles.summary: BBC Sport examines the potential benefits, risks and unanswered questions facing female athletes about egg-freezing.
articles.body:
"I remember waking up in the morning and I couldn't stand. I was bent over in two. I could barely walk."

For Geva Mentor - England netball's most decorated player - this was the reality of going through the process of having her eggs frozen in 2019.

"I had just played in my fourth World Cup and I was at a bit of a loss in terms of where my life was going personally, as I always wanted a family," Mentor tells BBC Sport.

Egg-freezing is a process in which a woman's eggs are collected, frozen and stored for potential use later in life.

While Mentor's decision was a deeply personal one, the issue is becoming increasingly visible in elite sport, with both Chelsea and the Spanish Football Federation recently announcing support for players wanting to freeze their eggs.

It is often presented as a way for women to help preserve their fertility and, in some cases, delay motherhood. For female athletes, whose careers often peak in the years they are most fertile, the appeal can be particularly powerful.

"I wanted to go through a check-up and make sure things weren't drying up down there, so to speak, because I didn't know what impact elite sport might have had on my fertility," says Mentor.

"Freezing my eggs seemed like the right thing to do at the time because [I thought] whatever happens with my journey, I'd rather use my early 30-year-old eggs than my late-30s or 40s."

Mentor is one of a growing number of athletes to consider fertility preservation during their careers, but the practice remains the subject of debate and experts stress it offers no guarantee of a future pregnancy.

England captain Jones calls for fertility support

Mentor is widely regarded as netball's greatest ever goal keeper, winning 175 international caps. She represented England at six World Cups, winning a silver and three bronze medals, and was part of the Roses side that won Commonwealth gold in 2018.

For 20 years, being an elite athlete was her every focus. However, she always knew she wanted to be a mother and worried about when that would come.

At the age of 35 she decided to freeze her eggs in the hope it may help her conceive in the future.

Mentor was not in a relationship at the time, and living in Melbourne.

"I decided that I wanted to do it in off-season, going into pre-season, and not during the season," she says.

"I thought that if anything untoward happened, I'd have that time and space to let my body recover before I'd have to sort of throw it into elite training."

Mentor had regular monitoring appointments throughout the treatment.

"I still trained, did pre-season," she adds. "It didn't affect me at all until I took the last reactive injection, which basically releases the eggs into position for extraction the next day."

Egg retrieval is performed under sedation or general anaesthetic and typically takes 15-30 minutes.

Mentor says it felt like she had "43 golf balls shoved in my lower region" as the fertility drugs she had taken had stimulated a large number of eggs, which were then retrieved.

"They pierced my vaginal wall 43 times, which meant that I was probably on a bit of a risk for bleeding and blood clots," she said.

"One of the things that really stood out for me was when I came around and I immediately just started crying... like bawling. It was quite emotional. What you're going through, that whole process, there's a lot of a hormone change and imbalance. I guess it really just shook me.

"But then I knew at the end of the day, it was an insurance policy for me."

Mentor was released from hospital the same day but was unable to return to full training for two weeks as she recovered from experiencing heavy bleeding.

She has since had a daughter after conceiving naturally but says she has no regrets about freezing her eggs, which remain available for her to use in the future.

While many have hailed fertility support for female athletes as a major step forward, one world-leading expert in women's health says important questions still remain.

Professor Kirsty Elliott-Sale, who heads the Centre for Excellence for Women in Sport at Manchester Metropolitan University, says she is "delighted for any player who will benefit" from fertility support.

But she believes egg-freezing should be seen as one option among a wider package of support for female athletes, and urges those considering it to look beyond the headlines - and ask plenty of questions.

"Egg-freezing is an opportunity which allows them to invest in their fertility journey - at this moment - for the future," she tells BBC Sport.

"But we need to make sure that if they want to have children during their careers, that is an opportunity for them."

Elliott-Sale says fertility, pregnancy and maternity provision must be as well funded as egg-freezing, so there is never a conversation that starts with: "Oh, but you froze your eggs..."

She also warns that egg-freezing should not be seen as a guarantee of future motherhood.

The number and quality of eggs collected can vary, some may not survive thawing, and those that do may fail to fertilise. Even when embryos develop, implantation and pregnancy are not assured.

There are also unanswered questions about how treatment fits around the demands of elite sport.

"One of the things that none of us know right now is how long you should take away from sport, if indeed you need to take any time away from sport to do this procedure," she says.

Elliott-Sale also wants clarity about what happens after eggs have been stored.

"It's one thing to fund the freezing," she says, questioning whether clubs will also pay for their storage then the treatment needed to use them.

And there's an anti-doping consideration, too.

Fertility drugs that are used to stimulate egg production for retrieval and freezing are banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency.

Athletes must therefore declare them and seek a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE), which gives them permission to take a prohibited substance for a specified time.

'You can't simply pause your career to become a mother'

Chelsea say their support extends beyond egg-freezing alone.

BBC Sport understands the club's fertility fund is worth £189,000, shared between 27 players - equivalent to £7,000 each.

A cycle of egg-freezing typically costs about £3,350, plus medication and ongoing storage fees. The full process, including thawing and embryo transfer, can cost £7,000-£8,000, according to UK regulator the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority.

Former Chelsea goalkeeper Carly Telford, now a commercial manager at the club, says players can access a range of services - from fertility testing and egg-freezing to IVF treatment.

"The players will have their own pot of money that's for them to use and dip into whenever they like," Telford said in an interview with CBS.

Players also have direct access to doctors and the clinic.

"I really hope that more clubs are looking at it," she added. "It's important for us to make sure we can be there and catch them when they need something else from us other than the football."

Spain international Alexia Putellas, meanwhile, welcomed her federation's fertility initiative as a "huge step forward".

Speaking to El Pais last month, she said: "The federation understands that you're serving your country at the expense of your biological clock… that you can't simply pause your career to become a mother because you need your body to do your job."

But Spanish Olympic triple jumper Ana Peleteiro-Compaore Brion questioned the motivation for the support.

"Is this measure intended to make it easier for women to be mothers or is it intended to make it easier for them not to be while they're playing?" she wrote on Instagram.

Elliott-Sale says the offer must be voluntary, properly explained and part of broader maternity support.

"I think for sure it's a great offer, it's a great choice and opportunity, but it needs to go alongside other considerations," she says.

articles.title: Father sold apartment, quit job; mother pledged gold: The making of Sahithi Varshini, India's latest WGM
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In May 2019, before the pandemic had pressed the pause button on the world, Sagar Shah, already an International Master (IM) and one of the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In May 2019, before the pandemic had pressed the pause button on the world, Sagar Shah, already an International Master (IM) and one of the most influential voices in today's chess fraternity, wrote a line in his ChessBase column: "Just like Humpy (Koneru) and Harika (Dronavalli) have made the world take note of Indian women's chess over the years, we have a feeling that within a few years Sahithi (Varshini Moogi) and Savitha (Shri Baskar) will also be right up there with the best in women's chess!"More than seven years have passed, and the same line reads less like a prediction and more like a question of legacy, much like asking whether Lamine Yamal could become the next Lionel Messi for Barcelona or whether Carlos Alcaraz could carry the torch of Spanish tennis after Rafael Nadal.Both girls are now 19. At the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand last month, Savitha added a team bronze to her growing list of accolades while also becoming the only Indian to win an individual gold medal at the event.Sahithi Varshini, on the other hand, has had a less decorated career so far. The Vizag-born prodigy recently became India’s latest Woman Grandmaster (WGM), a milestone by any measure. But is this the best she can do?"Whatever she has achieved so far, including this one (the WGM title), is not up to her potential. This is just a mere beginning," Lokeswara Moogi Rao, her father and only coach to date, told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction.The title and the three norms behind itJust last month, Sahithi's third and final WGM norm came at the IM VII Round Robin in Serbia. The 2007-born player finished second with 6/9, recorded a performance rating of 2408, and gained 23 rating points. That completed the requirements.The first two norms came in Hungary. The first was achieved at the Golden Horse IM Round Robin in September 2025, while the second came at the Kanizsa Open in August 2026, where she defeated GM Yeshaayahu Tzidkiya and recorded a performance rating of 2429.On paper, it may look like a clean progression. But the story behind it is much messier.To give a glimpse of how challenging it has been, when Sahithi was six, she caught dengue. She was on a ventilator for a week. She survived, and her family has always seen her recovery as a second life.What’s in the name?Long before chess became a part of his life, Lokeswara Moogi Rao, also known as Lokesh in the circuit, had discovered his passion in literature. During his college days, he spent hours immersed in English novels and occasionally tried his hand at writing. Years later, that love for literature would find its way into the name of his second daughter.“Sahithi is similar to Sahitya, which means literature,” Lokesh explained. But the name had another influence, one rooted in music.Lokesh comes from a family with a rich artistic background. His father’s side of the family was involved in theatre, and music was also part of their household. Lokesh himself was a keen singer, winning several prizes at the state level. Among the ragas he particularly admired was Amruthavarshini, whose name he wanted to draw upon for his daughter.His wife, however, felt that literature deserved a place in the name, too. And so, the two influences came together — Sahithi, inspired by literature, and Varshini, drawn from music.“But eventually, she didn’t belong to either of the two and chose the 64 squares,” Lokesh said with a smile. “She made a name for herself in a different domain.”Lokesh was born in a remote village on the edge of Yarada Hills, close enough to the sea that you could see it from the top. But there was no electricity. Before his father secured a job, the family had depended on fishing for a livelihood, as generations on his father’s side had done in a village near Srikakulam district. Walking to the next colony for food took half an hour.He still became a school topper and then a state-ranked student in the engineering entrance. But the family could not afford it. Lokesh's father had retired, and there was no financial backup. He left the course, took a small job after completing a diploma course, and finished an engineering degree by correspondence. Years later, he joined HPCL as an officer.How chess made entryLokesh was in his early 30s when he started taking chess seriously. He ran a literature club, a small group that exchanged idioms, short stories, and poems by email, trying to sharpen their English in Vizag.One member, Dinesh, a young medical student who lived opposite him, brought a huge chess trophy to the club one day after becoming the Andhra University chess champion. Having learnt that Lokesh had played chess as a child, Dinesh turned up at his house at ten one night with a chessboard.Lokesh's wife Jaya Sri, however, was left unimpressed, asking the two of them to play the game on the balcony.Lokesh was close to winning the first game and then collapsed. The next day Dinesh won two more. The day after, he won two again, and told Lokesh he had found his weakness. "I took it as a challenge," Lokesh recalled. "I wanted to win one game against him. That is how it started."He bought a book from a local shop and began reading in the refinery's control room, where officers sit around digital boards operating the plant. He would sketch positions on paper, then rub them out and redraw. A senior colleague, VS Prasad, caught him doing it and asked if he played chess. Lokesh begged him not to tell the bosses. Prasad took him home instead, to a shelf of 40 or 50 chess books.One was Max Euwe's The Road to Chess Mastery. For a man in love with literature, it certainly felt like a heaven. "It was like a Sherlock Holmes novel kind of a thing," he told this website.Soon, beating Dinesh became a routine. "I won some five to ten games straight away," he shared.Within three months, he made the HPCL team, and within six months of that he was at the national selections for the Petroleum Sports Promotion Board (PSPB), finishing second. He played for the board for roughly seven years, often captaining HPCL.At tournaments, he shared the hall with grandmasters such as Pentala Harikrishna, Shyam Sundar and Koneru Humpy, among others.He was never the strongest player in those rooms. Nevertheless, what he had was an appetite for classical chess. He would take an opening idea from a book, set up the position, and put it to the GMs. They told him he would one day be one of the finest coaches in the country."So that was the foundation," he said, giving us a touch of the philosophy behind Sahithi's approach today.A dream that wasn't a titleThe formal coach within Lokesh became active when her daughters started playing. Despite Sahithi showing early promise, he never set himself a target of IM or GM. What he wanted was a particular kind of game."I always had a very big dream to make her someone like Fischer and Kasparov, not a GM and all," he noted. "I never thought of making IM, GM and then celebrate it. Those moments are important, definitely, in life to cherish and move forward. But my dream was to make her someone like a legend."That ambition shows in how she plays. She goes for sacrifices and attacking positions, and her games grabbed early attention.At 14, she was rated over 2200. Her attacking play drew praise from Scottish Grandmaster, world-famous chess trainer, and author Jacob Aagaard. She also beat women's world champion Mariya Muzychuk."She never fears the opponent. She just plays her style," her coach said.Soon, she had also won a stack of age-group medals, among them Asian and Commonwealth golds.Three years the game took backThen came COVID. Sahithi was at her peak, rated highly and seeded at the top of her age groups, and the tournaments stopped. She missed almost three years of competitive chess."You are playing so well, and suddenly, you don't have the option of playing continuously," Lokesh said. "That was really annoying."Leave from work was a problem even before the pandemic. She qualified for a world youth championship (the Cadets tournament) but could not travel. After the lockdowns, Lokesh took long leave and moved the family abroad, reasoning that a rented apartment would cost less than repeated flights. It was a gamble, and he knew it.It also exposed a different problem. Online chess meant every game she played in open tournaments was published, and opponents could prepare against her at the click of a button. A player who loved to surprise people was suddenly easy to study. She tried switching openings from one day to the next, which backfired against stronger opposition.Playing 2300-rated players, he explained, you cannot get away with half-prepared systems. "It did backfire for almost a year," he said.But she came out of it understanding more openings than before. And in 2022 she played at the Chess Olympiad in Chennai, a member of India's C women's team and among the youngest in the squad. "Playing for India is always a special thing," Lokesh told this website.After the Olympiad, the targets slipped away. Sahithi secured a 13th-place finish at the FIDE Women's World Rapid Chess Championship 2023 held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, which also earned praise from former five-time world champion Viswanathan Anand. She was close to 2300 but not there, and the company could not keep granting leave.It cost Lokesh his jobThe trips abroad were expensive. HPCL contributed around Rs 10 lakh to Sahithi's career, and the Andhra Pradesh government gave a similar amount, but it was not enough."I had to sell an apartment," Lokesh revealed. His wife's gold was pledged. He was running out of options when he reached the most difficult decision almost three years back. "There was only one way. I had to quit my job," he recalled.He resigned and set up a chess academy, which he admits was harder than it sounded. A start in Hyderabad did not work for about ten months, partly because he was away at tournaments with Sahithi.Then, following a heart attack, he had a bypass operation, the heart surgery that forced him to stop for months and reduced both his income and his strength.Around the same time, relatives pressed him to make Sahithi finish class 10. She took nine months away from chess to do it."It sets the morale down," he said of the surgery. "Financially, it also consumes."Jaya Sri was a rock throughout. "I appreciate my wife more than me to be more braver than myself," he said. For a woman who was not earning and had no connection to chess, living with selling property, shifting country, and watching her husband leave his job, he considers it a far harder act of faith than his own.His elder daughter Falguni, now a FIDE arbiter, helped too, paying her own fees and rent by teaching classes.The decision to open the chess academy turned out better than he feared. Back in Visakhapatnam, the academy grew.His student Ajay santhosh Parvathareddy has amassed two GM norms and is now on the verge of beocoming a grand master. Aarav Sinha has collected four IM norms, and others gained hundreds of rating points within months on the European circuit. More than fifteen players now train with him, and he is writing a book on the 2200 level."After surgery, I have had bigger achievements compared to pre-surgery," he remarked.What comes nextSahithi was his first student. She remains the one he measures the rest against. But she is not, by his father's account, in the best place mentally."She is a little demotivated, to be frank," Lokesh added. The three lost years still weigh on her. Her advice, however, is the same every time."How you start is not as important as how you end," he tells her. "Whatever you missed in those years, no regrets for that. Just look at what opportunities you have."The plan is to build strength rather than chase a rating. "If you are 2500, you should be able to play like a 2500," he explained. "It should not merely happen with your rating. You should deserve it."There are no big names in this journey. No godfathers. You don't require big names to make your stamp.The harder obstacle is access. Official events such as the Asian Championships, Commonwealth events and World Juniors come with hotel costs that the family cannot easily meet. Lokesh believes that if Sahithi is given those platforms, results and sponsors will follow. If not, he will keep creating his own opportunities."I'm optimistic that way, rather than regretting not having big sponsors," he acknowledged, thanking Pravaha Foundation for currently sponsoring the chess prodigy in her journey."There are no big names in this journey. No godfathers. You don't require big names to make your stamp. It is your willpower, your passion for the game, your determination, and how you sustain in the difficult phases that take you forward."Perhaps Sagar Shah had got it right all those years ago. Like rice that takes time to cook to perfection over a gentle flame, Sahithi Varshini, too, may need time to come into her own. And when she does, it may well be to carry forward the legacy of those who came before her in chess, sooner rather than later.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: David Sánchez carga contra Gaspart por Messi: “Está mil pisos por debajo de Leo en la historia del Barça”
articles.standfirst: El periodista de Radio MARCA criticó el tono del expresidente azulgrana con la gran leyenda del Barça y pidió “un mínimo de cariño” para acercar posturas de cara a su homenaje pendiente
articles.summary: El periodista de Radio MARCA criticó el tono del expresidente azulgrana con la gran leyenda del Barça y pidió “un mínimo de cariño” para acercar posturas de cara a su homenaje pendiente
articles.body: David Sánchez puso el foco en Joan Gaspart y en sus palabras sobre Leo Messi. El periodista de Radio MARCA, en sus habituales Picotazos, reaccionó con dureza a la intervención del expresidente del Barcelona en el podcast Solo para culés, donde Gaspart recordó que “ni Leo Messi está por encima del FC Barcelona”. La respuesta de Sánchez no se centró tanto en discutir la idea de fondo como en la manera en la que Gaspart se dirigió al argentino. Para él, el barcelonismo puede debatir si Messi está por encima, por debajo o al mismo nivel que la institución, pero no desde cualquier tono ni desde cualquier altavoz. “Lo grave no es el fondo de lo que dice Joan Gaspart, que quizás puede o no tener razón. Lo grave es el tono con el cual se dirige Joan Gaspart a Leo Messi”, aseguró Sánchez. El periodista quiso separar el debate institucional de la forma elegida por el expresidente para referirse al futbolista más importante de la historia azulgrana. Sánchez admitió que no tiene “claro que Leo Messi sea más que el FC Barcelona” y dejó esa cuestión abierta a la opinión de cada barcelonista. Lo que sí cuestionó fue que Gaspart se colocara en posición de advertir al argentino, especialmente por el lugar que ocupa cada uno en la memoria reciente del club. El periodista entendió que la discusión sobre la grandeza de una entidad y la de su mejor futbolista puede tener matices. Otra cosa, según su análisis, es convertir ese debate en una llamada de atención pública a Messi, cuando el argentino no ha sido quien ha abierto esa comparación. Ahí llegó la frase más dura de su intervención. “Lo que es seguro es que Leo Messi, para la historia del Barcelona, es mucho más importante que el peor presidente de la historia del Barça, que es Joan Gaspart”, afirmó. Sánchez añadió que esa etiqueta ha sido repetida por muchos culés e incluso reconocida por el propio Gaspart. A partir de ahí, el periodista fue más allá: “No es nadie para decirle a Leo Messi que no está por encima del club”. Su argumento se apoyó en que Messi nunca se ha colocado públicamente en ese lugar. “Leo Messi no lo ha dicho, ni lo ha asegurado, ni lo ha sentido”, recalcó. Sánchez situó el foco en el valor histórico del argentino dentro del Barcelona. Messi no solo es el jugador más determinante que ha pasado por el club, sino una figura que cambió la dimensión deportiva de una época entera. Por eso, considera que el trato hacia él debería medirse con especial cuidado. Sánchez también recordó la salida del argentino del Barcelona y el daño que dejó aquel episodio. “A Messi lo echaron del Barcelona”, apuntó, antes de reclamar “un mínimo de cariño” para reconstruir puentes y facilitar un homenaje que considera pendiente. Para el periodista, el club debe cuidar la relación con su gran leyenda si quiere cerrar la historia como merece. Ese homenaje, todavía sin concretarse, aparece como una cuenta emocional del barcelonismo con el futbolista que marcó su era más brillante. El cierre de Sánchez fue rotundo. “Desconozco si Messi está al nivel, por debajo o por encima de la institución”, concluyó. “Lo que es seguro es que Joan Gaspart está mil pisos por debajo de Leo Messi en la historia del Barcelona”.

articles.title: Seahawks’ Mike Macdonald Makes Candid Admission After Loss to 49ers
articles.summary: The Seattle Seahawks defense had no answer for San Francisco 49ers wideout Mike Evans, who recorded seven receptions on 10 targets for 113 receiving yards, 1...
articles.body:
The Seattle Seahawks defense had no answer for San Francisco 49ers wideout Mike Evans, who recorded seven receptions on 10 targets for 113 receiving yards, 16.1 yards per reception, and one touchdown.

Moreover, it was the Evans show in Seattle, as neither tight end George Kittle nor any other wideout came close to producing what the veteran wideout did in Week 6. With Evans torching the Seahawks' Josh Jobe, the question is whether head coach Mike Macdonald should've provided help for Jobe.

On Oct. 12, Macdonald made an appearance on Seattle Sports and shared a blunt admission regarding whether he should've had a different approach to defending Evans, who was the go-to guy for 49ers QB Brock Purdy.

"I know Josh got beat a couple of times," Macdonald said. "We trust Josh to play press man-to-man. He's been doing it for two years now, and he's done it at a high level. When that happens, you're going to lose one-on-ones.

"As the play caller and the guy designing the defense, should I have helped out? Should I have given Josh more help in some of those situations? Yeah, I could have. There's reasons why we called certain things in certain situations, and sometimes I'm right and sometimes I'm not."

Mike Macdonald Still Trusts Josh Jobe After Loss to 49ers

Despite Evans' performance against Jobe and the Seahawks' secondary, Macdonald intends not to change his approach and still intends to continue to put players like Jobe in those one-on-one situations.

"When you're not in the perfect thing on where they want to go with where the ball's intended, then you're going to end up in some one-on-one matchups," Macdonald added. "Our guys have won plenty of those over the years, and we'll continue to put those guys in those situations.

"We trust our guys, and I think that there's always technique things that you can improve on, especially when you're in one-to-one, man-on-man situations. But we don't leave that game with any less trust in Josh."

It will be interesting to see if the Seahawks do keep that approach when they face the Niners and Evans again on Nov. 29.

Seahawks Defense Was Put in Challenging Situations

While Evans' performance for the 49ers was a reason for the Seahawks getting the loss, there was another issue that led to Seattle falling at home against the Niners.

Seattle Sports' Michael Bumpus noted that the defense, along with not being able to contain Evans, had trouble defending short fields as the 49ers didn't have to go that far to put up points on their first three scoring drives.

This defense has to defend short fields," Bumpus said in an Oct. 12 video for Seattle Sports . "On their first three scores, the Niners only had to travel about 30-plus yards. When you have a short field, you give the football to a guy like Brock Purdy, who's been really efficient this year; they're probably going to put points on the board. We said the same thing a couple of weeks ago with the Commanders . They have to fix that and fix it early before you get to Denver."

articles.title: Timberwolves head coach throws shade at former star while discussing LaMelo Ball addition
articles.summary: Minnesota Timberwolves coach Chris Finch’s admission about how LaMelo Ball has already impacted the franchise might be viewed as a shot at a former star. The...
articles.body:
Minnesota Timberwolves coach Chris Finch's admission about how LaMelo Ball has already impacted the franchise might be viewed as a shot at a former star.

The Timberwolves made one of the boldest trades of the summer when they acquired LaMelo Ball from the Charlotte Hornets. While Ball is an extremely talented point guard, he is yet to play a playoff game in the NBA, with the Wolves hoping he has an instant winning impact.

Ball's addition to the Timberwolves has led to an evident morale boost within the locker room, with head coach Chris Finch making a pointed remark about what the team lost and what it gained with Ball.

Chris Finch's comments about LaMelo Ball viewed as shade towards Julius Randle

Finch spoke about Ball's addition to the team before a preseason game against the New York Knicks, highlighting Ball's positive energy in the locker room matching that of franchise star Anthony Edwards.

"He's always in a great mood. Always comes in smiling. He and Anthony have a shared quality: they're really hard to stay mad at. And they do some things that you want to get mad at. They have a reflective joy."

However, Finch's assertion that the Wolves 'traded moodiness for giddiness' has many feeling that's a pointed reference to former Timberwolves star Julius Randle.

"We referred to ourselves as a moody team in the last couple of years, at times, and it's probably gotten in our way. We've traded moodiness for giddiness. So, we've gotta get to some sort of happy medium."

The Timberwolves salary-dumped Randle to the Brooklyn Nets in the offseason, getting nothing in return except the cap space to acquire Ball a few weeks later.

Another outgoing star, Naz Reid, was very well-liked within the Wolves organisation and by the fanbase, so many think this has to be about Randle.

Despite Randle averaging 21.1 points, 6.7 rebounds, and 5.0 assists in the regular season, his numbers dropped drastically to 16.0 points and 7.5 rebounds in the playoffs, with many theorising that Randle lost motivation in the postseason.

Finch did maintain he needed to find a middle ground between the lows of last season and the highs of this preseason, so he will have to be the steady rock in the locker room that keeps emotions and expectations tempered all season.

articles.title: NHL Insider Reveals Chances Of Connor Hellebuyck Landing With Metropolitan Team
articles.summary: One of the major storylines in the NHL through the early goings of the 2026-27 NHL season is Winnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck, who has won the Vezi...
articles.body:
One of the major storylines in the NHL through the early goings of the 2026-27 NHL season is Winnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck, who has won the Vezina Trophy as the League's best player at his position multiple times, requesting a trade and subsequently holding out of Training Camp and being suspended as a result.

Right now, the Jets are rolling forward with former Edmonton Oilers goaltender Stuart Skinner as their top man on the depth chart, while Hellebuyck remains suspended and has forfeited over $300,000 in salary so far.

Meanwhile, the New York Rangers have lost franchise goaltender Igor Shesterkin for the rest of the season because of a lower-body injury that will require surgery. Could the Rangers come calling for Hellebuyck?

NHL Insider Doesn't Believe Winnipeg Jets Goaltender Connor Hellebuyck Will Land With Rangers

While some have suggested that the Rangers could potentially target Hellebuyck to replace Shesterkin, NHL Insider Elliotte Friedman doesn't believe that it's feasible, mainly because both goaltenders have multiple years left on their respective deals.

"This had led to a lot of wild speculation… especially online, would Connor Hellebuyck be a fit for the Rangers. Don't expect it. I just don't think it matches up," he said.

"I don't think it works, particularly because both goalies would have long-term deals after this season if they were both there," Friedman added.

Despite the rising salary cap, Rangers GM Chris Drury won't have two goaltenders with a combined $20 million cap hit on his roster.

Hellebuyck is signed through 2031 with an $8.5 million salary cap hit, while Shesterkin signed the richest contract in the history of the NHL for a goaltender, an eight-year, $92.475 million deal with a salary cap hit of $11.56 million a season.

Jets Goalie Connor Hellebuyck Requested A Trade

Hellebuyck, who has played his entire NHL career with the Jets, requested a trade shortly after last season ended, but only went public with it recently.

So far, the Jets have not acquiesced to his trade request, and suspended him without pay after he failed to report to Training Camp; he has yet to appear with the club this season.

articles.title: Video shows Rams’ Alaric Jackson punching Bills’ Bradley Chubb after MNF
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Rams dropped a 37-34 game at home to the Buffalo Bills that included finger-pointing at the offensive line. Coach Sean McVay described one t...
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Rams dropped a 37-34 game at home to the Buffalo Bills that included finger-pointing at the offensive line . Coach Sean McVay described one thing that made him "pissed" amid a wild postgame environment that included a punch thrown by Rams lineman Alaric Jackson.

Video showed Jackson walking after Bills linebacker Bradley Chubb and blasting him in the face with a big right-hand shot.

Jackson is a 6-foot-7, 338-pound tackle. Chubb described what happened to the California Post afterward.

"It was a close game," he said. "And, you know, they always catch the second guy, so I let him swing and my teammates held me back and I just chilled."

The play happened after Josh Allen led his Buffalo Bills to the game-winning field goal, which came after Rams kicker Harrison Mevis' field goal was blocked. Fingers were pointed at several Rams after the game for the heart-wrenching loss including McVay and one of his assistant coaches .

Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford was surgical on the day, racking up 383 yards and three touchdowns including 138 yards passing to Puka Nacua, the Rams' star wide receiver. Stafford's performance earned a 'GOAT' comment from Allen , who shredded the Rams' Chris Shula-led defense on the ground with 121 yards and a touchdown.

Jackson will almost certainly face some kind of discipline for his action after Monday Night's game, which would be bad news for a Rams offense that badly needs his services. The defense must play better, and Stafford must continue his high-flying ways, heading into October 18's home game against the Cardinals if the Rams are to get back on track.

articles.title: Blake Corum maximizes his opportunities in Week 5
articles.summary: Blake Corum logged just eight touches versus the Bills, but he turned those into 72 yards and a score in a Week 5 defeat.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Rams RB Blake Corum had five carries, 19 yards, and a touchdown versus the Buffalo Bills in Week 5. Corum also caught three passes for 53 yards.

Why It Matters: Despite getting only eight touches -- compared to 22 for Kyren Williams -- Corum basically matched the lead back's production with 72 yards and a touchdown. It's clear at this point that in games that are one-sided, Corum will receive a workload that's comparable to Williams. It bigger spots and closer contests, however, Williams will get the majority of opportunities. That bodes well for Corum in Week 6 when the Rams take on the woeful Cardinals . Use Corum with confidence this weekend as an RB3/flex.

articles.title: Rams OL Steve Avila reveals key to getting LA offense back on track after 2-3 start
articles.summary: Los Angeles Rams left guard Steve Avila said avoiding self-inflicted mistakes is the key to getting the offense back on track after Monday’s 37-34 overtime l...
articles.body:
Los Angeles Rams left guard Steve Avila said avoiding self-inflicted mistakes is the key to getting the offense back on track after Monday's 37-34 overtime loss to the Buffalo Bills.

The Rams fell to 2-3 despite forcing overtime at SoFi Stadium.

Sports Central LA took to X, formerly Twitter, to share Avila's postgame comments to reporter Jaime Maggio about keeping the offense out of difficult down-and-distance situations.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"Yeah, it really just comes down to stop shooting ourselves in the foot. We got to stop putting ourselves behind the chains, you know. We saw what happened when we didn't do that. I'd like to think that you know things would have gone the other way if if that didn't happen. But you know, it's football; things happen, and it's all about how you respond. And I feel like we kind of responded well, you know, with stuff like that. And again, ultimately, we just came short."

Los Angeles committed 11 penalties for 84 yards, undermining an offense that produced strong individual performances from quarterback Matthew Stafford and wide receiver Puka Nacua.

Stafford completed 40 of 54 passes for 383 yards and three touchdowns. Nacua caught a career-high 17 passes for 138 yards and a touchdown.

Kyren Williams scored on a 1-yard run with five seconds remaining in regulation to force overtime. The Rams then received another opportunity when Nate Landman forced a James Cook fumble and Aaron Donald recovered it.

That possession ended with Greg Rousseau blocking Harrison Mevis' potential game-winning 48-yard field-goal attempt. Tyler Bass subsequently kicked a 45-yard field goal with 1:55 left in overtime to secure the Bills' win.

The Rams remain below .500 after another loss , with Avila identifying cleaner execution as the offense's priority.

articles.body:
Andrea Medina made her debut for Spain Women against the United States in what is turning into an excellent season for the defender.

Medina has played youth football for the Spanish national team while she was at Atletico Madrid.

Nonetheless, she secured a move to play for Manchester United in the summer and has truly prospered under her compatriot Eva Olid.

The defender has been a regular starter in the team and, despite playing as a full back earlier in the season, Medina is currently being used as an attacking winger.

This was evident as she scored her first goal for the club in a 2-1 win over West Ham United at the end of September.

Medina was also voted the club's Player of the Month in an outstanding first few weeks at the club.

The 22-year-old was called up to Spain's squad to face the United States in two friendlies and came off the bench in the first match.

Medina played 24 minutes, completing 91% of her passes and all of her cross attempts.

She did not have any shots or key passes in the match, though, as Spain came out on top as 2-0 winners.

The youngster made one interception and a clearance but did not win any of her three duel attempts.

The 23-year-old also played 73 minutes of action in Canada Women's 3-4 loss to Denmark.

Awujo did not make any key passes and only completed 76% of her passing attempts.

She also failed to have a shot on goal and was ineffective in duels, winning just one of her six attempts.
